sentences.text: Hello and welcome to the Slow English podcast.
My name is Emily.
I am happy you are here.
Today we will talk about Ireland.
Ireland is a small and green country in Europe.
Let's learn about it in slow and easy English.
Are you ready?
Let's begin.
Where is Ireland?
Ireland is in Western Europe.
It is an island in the Atlantic Ocean.
To the east of Ireland is the United Kingdom.
Ireland is sometimes called the Emerald Isle.
That means the green island
because it has green fields and rain.
What is the capital city of Ireland?
The capital city is Dublin.
Dublin is on the east coast near the sea.
It is the biggest city in Ireland.
Many people live there.
Dublin has museums, music, pubs and a long river called the Liffy.
It is full of history, stories and culture.
Other cities in Ireland include Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford.
How many people live in Ireland?
About 5 million people live in Ireland.
It is not a very big country.
Most people live in towns and cities.
But many also live in small villages and farms.
Ireland is known for being friendly and peaceful.
What language do people speak in Ireland?
People speak English in Ireland.
English is the main language.
But some people also speak Irish or Gaelge.
Irish is the original Celtic language of Ireland.
At school, children learn Irish as a subject.
In some areas, people speak Irish every day.
These places are called Geltacht.
What is the weather like in Ireland?
The weather in Ireland is often mild, cool and wet.
It rains often, but not too much at once.
There are many cloudy days, but also sunshine.
It does not get very hot in summer.
It does not get very cold in winter.
Snow is rare, but sometimes falls in the hills.
Because of the rain, the land stays green all year.
What does Ireland look like?
Ireland has green fields, hills, forests, and lakes.
There are also cliffs, beaches, and mountains.
One famous place is the cliffs of Mohar.
Tall cliffs above the sea.
Ireland has many rivers and islands.
It is a great place for walking, hiking, and exploring nature.
What animals live in Ireland?
In Ireland, you can see sheep, cows, and horses on farms,
foxes, hairs, and badgers in the countryside.
Many birds, such as swans, robins, and crows.
There are no snakes in Ireland.
That's a fun fact.
Legend says St. Patrick drove them away long ago.
What do people eat in Ireland?
Irish food is warm and simple.
People eat a lot of potatoes, bread, meat, and vegetables.
Some traditional foods are Irish stew, meat, potatoes, and carrots in a hot soup,
box-deep potato pancakes.
Soda bread, bread made without yeast.
Called cannon, mashed potatoes with cabbage,
seafood, especially in coastal towns.
For dessert, people eat apple tart, scones, or pudding.
They drink tea every day, often with milk.
What is life like in Ireland?
Life in Ireland is peaceful and relaxed.
People enjoy time with family and friends.
They like to talk, walk, read, and listen to music.
In the evenings, many people go to pubs.
They listen to traditional Irish music, drink tea or beer, and talk with friends.
People enjoy sports like football, rugby, and hurling, an Irish stick-and-ball game.
What are some Irish traditions and holidays?
St. Patrick's Day is on March 17.
People wear green, go to parades, and celebrate Irish culture.
Christmas is celebrated with family, food, and music.
In some areas, people still tell old stories and folktales about fairies and magic.
Traditional Irish dancing is fast and fun.
Dancers move their feet quickly, often in groups.
Some fun facts about Ireland.
The flag of Ireland is green, white, and orange.
Ireland is part of the European Union and uses the Euro.
Irish people love music, poetry, and storytelling.
Ireland has many famous writers, like James Joyce and Oscar Wilde.
The harp is the national symbol of Ireland.
Many movies are filmed in Ireland because of its beautiful scenery.
Now you know many things about Ireland.
You know where it is, what people speak, and what the weather is like.
You learned about Irish food, music, animals, and traditions.
Good job!
Goodbye, or as they say in Irish, slán.
